question: A 71-year-old man presents to the physician for a routine health-maintenance examination. He feels well; however, he is concerned about the need for prostate cancer screening. He has a 3-year history of benign prostatic hyperplasia. His symptoms of urinary hesitancy and terminal dribbling of urine are well controlled with tamsulosin and finasteride. He also had a percutaneous coronary angioplasty done 2 years ago following a diagnosis of unstable angina. His medication list also includes aspirin, atorvastatin, losartan, and nitroglycerin. His vital signs are within normal limits. He has never had a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test or prostate ultrasonography. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for prostate cancer in this patient?

CHAIN: "Patient feels well and has controlled urinary symptoms" -> "No immediate symptoms of prostate cancer" -> "Screening is still recommended due to age" -> "Serum PSA testing is a standard approach" -> "Serum PSA every 2-4 years is appropriate" -> 80%
analysis: The patient is a 71-year-old man who has never had a PSA test. Current guidelines from organizations such as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommend that men aged 55 to 69 discuss the potential benefits and harms of PSA screening with their physician. For men aged 70 and older, the recommendation is less clear, and many guidelines suggest that routine screening may not be necessary, especially if the patient has a limited life expectancy or other significant health issues. Given that this patient is asymptomatic and has no prior PSA testing, the most appropriate approach would be to avoid routine screening unless there are specific risk factors or symptoms that warrant it. Therefore, the best-supported option is to recommend no screening test at this time.
